Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty Images Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6. Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs. The latest benefit changes build on Walmart's years-long effort to boost employee compensation after previously receiving criticism for the healthcare benefits and wages it offers. Walmart employs roughly 2.1 million associates worldwide, with about 1.6 million of those workers based in the U.S., as of the end of fiscal year 2026. In a statement, the company said it's minimizing premium increases for its employees, raising rates for its starting plan by $1.50 per pay period to $39.80. Walmart told CNBC that's a smaller increase than the company made last year. The company is also expanding an existing benefit that pays for employees to see cancer specialists at the Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic, according to a Tuesday letter to workers from Donna Morris, Walmart's chief people officer. Starting next year, employees under most plans can use that benefit to get a second opinion from a specialist for rare conditions such as ALS, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's. Among the other added benefits is up to 12 weeks of neonatal intensive care unit leave for parents, which can be added on top of regular parental and maternity leave, the letter said. "The steps we're taking are based on years of planning and trying new things, which is allowing us to make meaningful improvements for associates without slashing benefits or significantly raising premiums," Walmart said in its statement to CNBC. headlines.article_text: JPMorgan blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from account access Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of rogue agents operating at scale and said the bank is building defensive tools. The bank is piloting Smart Cash, an internal tool to forecast cash flow and move funds to maximize yield. Dimon said customers using outside agents must understand the risks and potential transfer of responsibility. In this article JPM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan (L), and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta. Getty Images JPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call. "You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers. The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers. "Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said. "We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added. That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, like customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful. There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added. 'Liability transfer' Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely. In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, CFO Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents. Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer." Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example. Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month. In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts. headlines.article_text: Boeing delivers 57 jets in September Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article BA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Boeing Co. 737 Max airplane at the company's manufacturing facility in Renton, Washington, US, on Thursday, Nov. 20, 2025. David Ryder | Bloomberg | Getty Images Boeing said on Tuesday that it delivered 57 jets in September, up from 51 in August and 55 a year earlier as it works to ramp up production of its best-selling 737 MAX narrow-body. Turkish Airlines' order for 100 737 MAX jets boosted Boeing's September total of new orders to 165. The US planemaker still trailed European rival Airbus' 72 deliveries in September, but Boeing far outsold its rival, which booked only 17 new orders from two customers last month. Boeing's September deliveries included 43 737 MAX jets, eight 787s, two 777 freighters and four 767s, including three for Boeing's defense unit for completion as KC-46 aerial refueling tankers. The higher deliveries come as Boeing works to consistently increase 737 MAX output to 47 jets a month, which has taken longer than expected, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said during an investor conference in September. Through September, Boeing has delivered 475 jets this year, up 8% from a year earlier. That includes 363 737 MAX jets, the most the MAX program has ever delivered in the first nine months of a year. In addition to Turkish Airlines' order, Boeing booked orders for 20 737 MAX jets for Lufthansa, six 737 MAX and five 787 jets for Biman Bangladesh Airlines, and eight 777-8 freighters and two 777 freighters for Ethiopian Airlines. Another six 737 MAX and 18 787 orders came from unidentified customers. Boeing ended September with an official backlog of 6,371 jets, up from 6,156 at the end of August. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:47 03:47 Apple announces new home products: Here's what you need to know TechCheck Apple on Tuesday announced a new home hub called HomeView . Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said that HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. Apple's HomeView can be placed on a table or mounted on a wall. Apple "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's chief marketer Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. The Apple HomeView, an iPad-like device meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops that will showcase its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant, during a launch of smart home products in New York City, US, October 13, 2026. Shannon Stapleton | Reuters Apple said on Tuesday that its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales but also helps further lock customers into its own ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. It also comes as new boss Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster. MedTech soft spot Medical technology division sales rose 2.5% to $8.6 billion overall, missing analysts' estimates of $8.71 billion, according to LSEG data. Outside the U.S., the division's sales were essentially flat. "Our performance is below the standard we have set internally and below the expectations we previously communicated to investors," said Tim Schmid, J&J's medical technology chief. "Simply put, we can do better," he said, adding that the company was focused on improving fourth-quarter performance. He said the environment for medical procedures remains stable in key markets. Shares of other medical device makers were also lower, with Boston Scientific down nearly 3% and Intuitive Surgical shares off about 2%. But J.P. Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus said it's hard to generalize J&J's results to the rest of the medtech sector, given company-specific disruption from China supply, the pending orthopedics unit spin-off, and likely greater exposure to disruption in the Middle East. Hips and knee spinoff The company said late last year it intended to spin off its orthopedics unit, DePuy Synthes, into a standalone company, marking its second major spinoff as it sharpens its focus on higher-growth healthcare segments. Wolk, on a conference call to discuss company results, said J&J remains on track for a mid-2027 separation. "Given the way DePuy Synthes is performing... we are leaning towards a spin as being the best option to create long-term value for Johnson & Johnson shareholders. That has always been our base plan, and we are confident that it can be successfully executed," he said. Daniel Barasa, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, said depressed medtech valuations "probably made it harder to complete a sale of the orthopedic business, which may also be weighing on the stock." J&J raised its full-year forecast for reported sales to about $101.2 billion at the midpoint, up from $101.1 billion. It increased its adjusted earnings forecast range with a new midpoint of $11.10 per share, up from $11.04. Quarterly pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% to $16.76 billion. Sales of Tremfya for Crohn's disease and other autoimmune conditions rose 68% to $2.4 billion, exceeding analyst estimates of about $2.2 billion, while sales of Stelara, which is facing generic competition, fell 54% to $716 million, still well above diminished Wall Street expectations of $591 million. Tremfya has increasingly replaced lost Stelara revenue following recent approvals in inflammatory bowel diseases. Sales of blood cancer treatment Darzalex rose about 16% to $4.24 billion, short of analyst expectations of $4.4 billion. headlines.article_text: Bank earnings October 2026: JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo, Citigroup Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Four of the largest U.S. banks reported third-quarter results on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo , Goldman Sachs and Citigroup . Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday. The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs. The banks that reported Tuesday put up mixed results . JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets and the largest in the world by market capitalization, posted a rare miss. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, blew past estimates for revenue and earnings per share, led by strong equities trading. Analyst calls for all four banks touched on the opportunities and risks associated with AI, citing robust financing demand and operational advantages, but also the threat of rogue agents. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon also addressed recent reports of a CEO transition plan, and Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo joined CNBC to discuss the firm's growth and the state of the consumer. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report on Wednesday to round out third-quarter results for the major U.S. firms. — Sara Salinas 3 Hours Ago Wells Fargo CFO says consumer is doing well watch now VIDEO 5:04 05:04 Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo: Consumer is doing well Squawk on the Street Wells Fargo's Santomassimo told CNBC that both consumers and businesses are doing "really well." "I think despite higher gas prices, both sides of the equation have been able to really work through that," he said. "We're just not seeing any sort of cracks around delinquency trends that would lead you to believe you're going to see any near-term stress that come through, at least at least for now." – Laya Neelakandan 3 Hours Ago Wells Fargo CFO to CNBC: Momentum is growing Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the company's underlying results are "really good" and that the bank is seeing "continued momentum" across all of its businesses. "As you look at the net interest margin, what that really shows is sort of this good stabilization of the underlying trends," he said. "You see the higher rate environment starting to come through in terms of helping it as you look forward, and so for us, the opportunity we have ahead of us is just as big as it was last quarter." VIDEO 6:23 06:23 Watch CNBC’s full interview with Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo – Laya Neelakandan 4 Hours Ago Citi sees consumer continuing to drive growth Jane Fraser, chief executive officer of Citigroup Inc., during a Bloomberg Television interview on the sidelines of the Citi China Conference in Shanghai, China, on Friday, Nov. 14, 2025. Qilai Shen | Bloomberg | Getty Images Citi's Fraser said on the call with analysts that macro environment conditions softened during the third quarter and that the "global economy has held up remarkably well." "In the U.S., while much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much of the growth," she said. "The labor market is stable, and companies remain active. Our near-term economic outlook remains positive." She added that the bank's clients have remained "engaged" and "healthy." – Laya Neelakandan 4 Hours Ago Citi CEO: Cyberdefense is a priority Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said on a call with analysts on Tuesday that the company is focused on reducing systemic risk while deploying AI firm-wide. "Our cyberdefense strategy is about being on the front foot, about moving fast and retaining trust," Fraser said. "We don't wait for risks to happen. We're constantly preparing and improving our defenses. We're in the business of managing risk everyday, and this is no different." – Laya Neelakandan 4 Hours Ago Investment banking fees mostly hold up watch now VIDEO 3:52 03:52 Goldman Sachs CEO says IPO market was 'a little bit softer in September' Squawk on the Street Investment banking fees at all four firms reporting on Tuesday largely held up during the third quarter, with most firms either matching or surpassing prior guidance. Still, the reports revealed declines on a quarter-over-quarter basis. At JPMorgan, investment banking revenue was up 14% year over year but down 8% quarter over quarter. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline remains "very, very strong." Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon echoed that sentiment on his company's analyst call, while declining to say whether capital markets activity has peaked. That bank reported fees that were 21% higher from the prior year, but 5% lower than the second quarter. "IPOs that came in September were really the result of conversations in May and June around valuation expectations. Things got a little bit softer in September," Solomon said. "The IPO market was wide open. It's just if you expected a valuation and you got something 10 %to 15% less, you might choose not to go forward, you might choose to wait." Solomon added all the tech innovation and the AI infrastructure activity is a "real good ballast" for capital markets activity on a go-forward basis, noting that doesn't mean there won't be bumps. Citi posted the largest quarter-over-quarter decline in the fees, at 13% down. Wells Fargo reported investment banking revenue that was down 5% from the prior quarter. — Leslie Picker 4 Hours Ago Goldman Sachs CEO sees growing risks in financing the AI infrastructure buildout Goldman Sachs Chairman and CEO David Solomon speaks at the Economic Club of New York in New York City, on June 2, 2026. Angela Weiss | AFP | Getty Images Solomon warned that the AI infrastructure boom could face a painful reset if higher borrowing costs or overbuilding undermine the economics of some data center projects. "There is going to be a lot of financing to do, and we're going to be in the middle of that," Solomon said during the bank's third-quarter call. "It may be that over time as the financing needs grow, that there's pressure on rates and that will affect the returns and the viability of certain projects," he said. "Not every project is going to be received as well." For now, demand for computing power remains strong and supply has yet to catch up, Solomon said, meaning more infrastructure will be built and more financing from Goldman and others will be needed. It's impossible to predict when a reset might happen or how the technology would evolve and be deployed, he said, calling the dynamic "an unknown we have to live with." "There will be a point in time when this recalibration resets, for sure," Solomon said. "When that does happen, of course there'll be some bumps." — Hugh Son 4 Hours Ago Citigroup is beginning its conference call with analysts Citigroup, the final bank of the morning, is beginning its conference call with executives and analysts to discuss its third-quarter earnings results. – Laya Neelakandan 4 Hours Ago Goldman CEO David Solomon denies succession plans are in motion John Waldron, chief operating officer of Goldman Sachs Group Inc., and Goldman Sachs Chairman and CEO David Solomon.
